items.title: Central Asian Contacts after the Mauryas
items.body:
## A Melting Pot in the North-West (c. 200 BCE – early CE)

- After the **decline of the Mauryan Empire**, several Central Asian dynasties — the **Indo-Greeks, Shakas (Scythians), Parthians (Pahlavas), and Kushanas** — replaced the Mauryan rulers in **north-western India**.
- These dynasties introduced new elements in **politics, trade, religion, art, and architecture**.
- The interaction with Central Asia enriched Indian culture, making it a **melting pot** of various traditions and ideas.
- Central Asian rulers **integrated with Indian society** by adopting local customs, languages, and religions, leaving a profound impact on Indian civilization.
- The usual order of arrival was **Indo-Greeks → Shakas → Parthians → Kushanas**.
keyPoints: Four Central Asian powers followed the Mauryas in the NW: Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas.
They enriched Indian politics, trade, religion, art and architecture.
Rulers assimilated by adopting local customs, languages and religions.
Typical order of arrival: Indo-Greeks → Shakas → Parthians → Kushanas.
items.mnemonic: Arrival order 'GSPK' — Greeks, Shakas, Parthians, Kushanas.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Central Asian Contacts)

items.title: Shakas (Scythians): Origin & Arrival
items.body:
## Who Were the Shakas?

- The **Shakas** were originally a **nomadic tribe from Central Asia**, driven towards India due to **wars with the Chinese and other tribes**.
- They were **displaced by the Yuezhi** and other Central Asian groups, and settled in various parts of India.
- Shakas controlled vast territories including parts of **Gujarat, Punjab, Mathura, and the Deccan**.
- The Indo-Greeks' last ruler **Hermaius** was defeated by the Parthians, and Greek control in the north-west declined, making way for **Shaka and Parthian rule**.
keyPoints: Shakas = nomadic Scythian tribe from Central Asia, pushed into India after wars with the Chinese.
Displaced by the Yuezhi and other Central Asian groups.
Held territory in Gujarat, Punjab, Mathura and the Deccan.
Filled the vacuum left by declining Indo-Greek (Hermaius) rule.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Shakas / Scythians)

items.title: The Five Branches of the Shakas
items.body:
## Shaka Political Divisions

The Shakas ruled through five regional branches:

1. **1st Branch — Afghanistan:** rulers **Vonones, Spalirises**; established the initial north-west presence.
2. **2nd Branch — Punjab:** ruler **Maues**, capital **Taxila**; strengthened the foothold in Punjab.
3. **3rd Branch — Mathura:** ruler **Azilises**; ruled for nearly two centuries.
4. **4th Branch — Gujarat & Western India:** ruler **Rudradaman I**, capital **Ujjain**; issued Sanskrit inscriptions and repaired Sudarshana Lake.
5. **5th Branch — Upper Deccan (Andhra & Maharashtra):** established regional rule in the Deccan.

figure.alt: Map of the Indo-Scythian (Shaka) Kingdom showing Taxila, Sagala, Mathura, Ujjain and the Western Satraps
figure.caption: The Indo-Scythian (Shaka) Kingdom stretched across the north-west and Western India, with the Western Satraps centred on Ujjain and reaching Mathura, Taxila and Barigaza.

keyPoints: Five branches: Afghanistan (Vonones/Spalirises), Punjab (Maues, Taxila), Mathura (Azilises), Gujarat/W. India (Rudradaman I, Ujjain), Upper Deccan.
Maues used Taxila as his capital in Punjab.
The Mathura branch (Azilises) endured for nearly two centuries.
The most important branch was the Western Indian one under Rudradaman I at Ujjain.
items.mnemonic: Branch capitals north→south — 'Afghanistan, Taxila, Mathura, Ujjain, Deccan'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Political History of the Shakas)

items.title: Rudradaman I & the Junagadh (Girnar) Rock Inscription
items.body:
## The Greatest Shaka Ruler (130–150 CE)

- **Rudradaman I** was the **most powerful Shaka ruler**, expanding into **Gujarat, Sindh, Kutch, Kathiawar, and parts of the Deccan**.
- He **defeated the Satavahana kings** and consolidated power over **Konkan and Malwa**.
- He issued the **first long inscription in chaste Sanskrit** — the **Junagadh / Girnar Rock Inscription** — a landmark in the use of Sanskrit for royal records.
- The inscription records his **repair of the Sudarshana Lake** in Kathiawar (originally built in Mauryan times), demonstrating concern for **public welfare**.
- Despite his Central Asian origin, he was a great **patron of Sanskrit language and culture**.
keyPoints: Rudradaman I (130–150 CE) — the most powerful Shaka ruler; capital Ujjain.
Defeated the Satavahanas; held Gujarat, Sindh, Kutch, Kathiawar, Konkan, Malwa.
Junagadh/Girnar Rock Inscription = the first long inscription in chaste Sanskrit.
The inscription records repair of the Sudarshana Lake in Kathiawar.
A Central Asian ruler who championed Sanskrit language and culture.
items.mnemonic: Rudradaman 'RSS' — Rudradaman, Sanskrit (first long), Sudarshana Lake.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Rudradaman I)

items.title: Chastana & the Western Kshatrapas
items.body:
## The Western Kshatrapa Dynasty

- **Chastana** established the **Western Kshatrapa dynasty** with its centre at **Ujjain**.
- His successors — including **Rudradaman I** — ruled parts of **Malwa and Gujarat** for several generations.
- Other prominent early Shaka rulers include:
  - **Maues (Moga):** ruled Punjab and Gandhara (1st century BCE); issued coins depicting Greek deities like **Zeus and Athena**; adopted Hellenistic governance and supported Buddhism.
  - **Azilises:** strengthened Shaka control over **Mathura** and continued minting **bilingual coins** in the Indo-Greek tradition.
keyPoints: Chastana founded the Western Kshatrapa dynasty, based at Ujjain.
The dynasty (incl. Rudradaman I) ruled Malwa and Gujarat for generations.
Maues (Moga) issued coins with Greek deities (Zeus, Athena) and backed Buddhism.
Azilises consolidated Mathura and continued bilingual Indo-Greek-style coinage.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Prominent Shaka Rulers)

items.title: The Satrap System & Administration
items.body:
## Governance under the Shakas

- The Shakas introduced the **satrap system**, dividing the empire into smaller regions called **satrapies**.
- **Satraps (governors)** were appointed to manage local governance, ensuring control over distant regions.
- **Military governance** was a hallmark of Shaka rule, inherited from the Indo-Greeks.
- They **minted coins in large quantities**, using **bilingual inscriptions (Greek and Prakrit)** for administrative coherence.

### Administrative Titles

- **Satrap** — military governor of a province.
- **Kshatrapa** — junior satrap with delegated responsibilities.
- **Mahasenapati** — supreme commander of the military forces.
- **Raja** — regional king responsible for governance.
keyPoints: Satrap system divided the empire into satrapies run by governors.
Rule was strongly military in character, inherited from the Indo-Greeks.
Large-scale coinage carried bilingual Greek + Prakrit legends.
Title ladder: Satrap → Kshatrapa (junior) → Mahasenapati (commander) → Raja (regional king).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Governance and Administration)

items.title: Eras: Vikram Samvat (58 BCE) & Saka Era (78 CE)
items.body:
## Two Calendars Linked to the Shakas

- **Vikram Samvat (58 BCE):** around 58 BCE a local ruler known as **Vikramaditya** is said to have **defeated the Shakas** and established the **Vikram Samvat** era to mark the victory.
- **Saka Era (78 CE):** the **Saka era** — beginning in **78 CE** — is the great dating era associated with the Shaka/Western Kshatrapa period; it later became the basis of the **Indian national calendar (Saka Samvat)**.
- Both eras are still widely referenced in Indian chronology and inscriptions.
- Note the direction: **Vikram Samvat counts from 58 BCE**, while the **Saka era counts from 78 CE** (a 135-year gap).
keyPoints: Vikram Samvat began 58 BCE after Vikramaditya's victory over the Shakas.
The Saka era began in 78 CE and underlies the modern Indian national calendar.
Vikram Samvat (58 BCE) is earlier than the Saka era (78 CE) by 135 years.
Both eras remain standard reference points in Indian chronology.
items.mnemonic: 'Vikram before, Saka after' — Vikram 58 BCE, Saka 78 CE.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Decline of the Shakas — Vikramaditya/Vikram Samvat); Saka era 78 CE is a standard, widely-accepted chronological fact.

items.title: Society, Culture & Religion under the Shakas
items.body:
## Assimilation into Indian Society

- **Cultural assimilation:** despite their Central Asian origin, the Shakas integrated into Indian society, embracing customs and religions like **Hinduism and Buddhism**.
- **Intermarriage:** marriage alliances with local rulers were common (e.g., **Rudradaman's alliance with the Satavahanas**); Shakas were gradually absorbed into the **Kshatriya (warrior) class**.
- **Manusmriti** describes the Shakas as **fallen Kshatriyas** who had lost their original status.
- **Religious patronage:** many rulers adopted **Buddhism**, while others worshipped Hindu deities like **Shiva and Vishnu** and patronized **Vaishnavism**; the Shakas promoted **religious tolerance**.
- Militarily they introduced **advanced cavalry tactics** (saddles, reins) and popularized **long coats, trousers, and boots**.
keyPoints: Shakas assimilated into Indian society, adopting Hinduism and Buddhism.
Intermarriage (Rudradaman–Satavahana) absorbed them into the Kshatriya class.
Manusmriti calls the Shakas 'fallen Kshatriyas'.
Patronised Shiva, Vishnu (Vaishnavism) and Buddhist monasteries; promoted tolerance.
Introduced cavalry tactics (saddles, reins) and trousers, coats and boots in warfare.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Society and Culture / Religion under Shakas)

items.title: Parthians (Pahlavas): Origin & Rule
items.body:
## The Pahlavas in India

- The **Parthians** originally came from **Iran and Central Asia**.
- Ancient **Sanskrit texts** mention them along with the Shakas as **"Shaka-Pahlavas"**.
- They established their presence in **north-western India** after the decline of Indo-Greek rule and alongside Shaka domination.
- Their **political control was limited**, but they integrated into Indian society and promoted **Indian religions and art**.
- Early Parthian rulers include **Vonones** (Afghanistan) and **Spalirises** (Gandhara and Taxila), who strengthened the Parthian foothold in the north-west.

figure.alt: Map of the Parthian Empire showing the Pahlavas (Indo-Parthia) between Persia, Bactria, the Sakas and the Kushans
figure.caption: The Parthian Empire and the Pahlavas (Indo-Parthia) lay between Persia and the Indian north-west, neighbouring the Sakas, Bactria and the rising Kushans.

keyPoints: Parthians (Pahlavas) originated in Iran and Central Asia.
Sanskrit texts group them with the Shakas as 'Shaka-Pahlavas'.
Entered NW India after the Indo-Greek decline, alongside Shaka power.
Political control was limited but they promoted Indian religions and art.
Early rulers: Vonones (Afghanistan), Spalirises (Gandhara/Taxila).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Parthians / Pahlavas)

items.title: Gondophernes & the St Thomas Tradition
items.body:
## The Most Prominent Parthian Ruler (19–45 CE)

- **Gondophernes** was the most prominent Parthian ruler, with his rule centred on **Taxila** (modern Pakistan).
- **Religion:** he is traditionally said to have been **converted to Christianity by St Thomas the Apostle**, who came to India to spread Christianity — one of the earliest Christian influences in India.
- **Buddhism:** he patronized **Buddhist monasteries and built stupas**.
- **Coins & inscriptions:** he issued coins with **Greek legends and Indian symbols**, reflecting a blend of cultures.
- **Takht-i-Bahi Inscription:** found near **Mardan** and dated to **45 CE**, it provides valuable information about his reign.
- His successor **Abdagases** lost much of the territory to the **Kushanas**.

figure.alt: Ruins of the Takht-i-Bahi Buddhist monastery near Mardan, associated with the Parthian period
figure.caption: The hilltop Buddhist monastery ruins at Takht-i-Bahi (near Mardan) — the nearby Takht-i-Bahi inscription of 45 CE dates the reign of Gondophernes.

keyPoints: Gondophernes (19–45 CE) — most prominent Parthian ruler; capital Taxila.
Tradition holds he was converted to Christianity by St Thomas — an early Christian link to India.
Patronised Buddhist monasteries and built stupas.
Coins carried Greek legends with Indian symbols (cultural blend).
Takht-i-Bahi inscription (45 CE, near Mardan) documents his reign; Abdagases succeeded him and lost land to the Kushanas.
items.mnemonic: Gondophernes 'GST' — Gondophernes, St Thomas, Takht-i-Bahi (45 CE).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Maurya - Sakas and Parthians (Gondophernes and His Legacy)

items.title: Decline of the Shakas & Parthians
items.body:
## How Their Rule Ended

- **Rise of local dynasties:** the **Satavahanas** and later the **Guptas** launched campaigns to drive the Shakas out of their territories.
- **Defeat by Vikramaditya:** around **58 BCE**, the ruler **Vikramaditya** defeated the Shakas and established the **Vikram Samvat** era.
- **Displacement by the Kushanas:** the **Kushanas** eventually displaced both the Shakas and the Parthians in north-western India; the last Parthian rulers were absorbed into Kushan governance.
- **Assimilation:** over time both groups lost their distinct identity and became part of Indian culture and society (**Manusmriti** treats both as fallen Kshatriyas).
keyPoints: Satavahanas and Guptas campaigned to push the Shakas out.
Vikramaditya defeated the Shakas c. 58 BCE and founded the Vikram Samvat era.
The Kushanas displaced both Shakas and Parthians in the NW.
Both groups were finally assimilated into Indian society (fallen Kshatriyas).

items.title: Precision Facts the PYQs Hinge On (Junagadh, Vikramaditya, Gandhara)
items.body:
## High-Yield Exam Nuggets

### The Junagadh (Girnar) Rock — THREE rulers, one rock
The same rock at Junagadh (Girnar, Gujarat) carries inscriptions of **three rulers across seven centuries**:

| Ruler | Date | Content |
|---|---|---|
| **Ashoka** | c. 250 BCE | His **14 Major Rock Edicts** (in Prakrit, Brahmi) |
| **Rudradaman I** | c. 150 CE | **First long inscription in chaste Sanskrit** (Brahmi script, **NOT Kharoshti**); records Sudarshana Lake repair |
| **Skandagupta** | c. 455–458 CE | Records **another repair** of the Sudarshana Lake dam after a flood |

### Sudarshana Lake — the details examiners test
- The lake was **originally built under Chandragupta Maurya** (by governor Pushyagupta) and improved under Ashoka.
- Rudradaman's record says he repaired it **from his own treasury, without imposing forced labour (vishti) or fresh taxes** on his subjects — the repair was executed by his Pahlava governor **Suvishakha**.

### 'Vikramaditya' and the Shakas
- Legend credits the **Vikram Samvat (58 BCE)** to a ruler titled **Vikramaditya** who beat the Shakas.
- Historically, the Gupta emperor **Chandragupta II adopted the title 'Vikramaditya'** and the epithet **'Sakari' (destroyer of the Shakas)** after conquering the **Western Kshatrapas** (c. 409 CE) — this ended Shaka rule in western India.

### Gandhara art
- The **Gandhara school** of sculpture that flourished in the north-west under Shaka–Parthian and (mainly) **Kushana** patronage drew heavily on **Greco-Roman (Hellenistic)** style — realistic drapery, wavy hair, muscular Buddha figures.
keyPoints: Junagadh/Girnar rock bears inscriptions of THREE rulers: Ashoka, Rudradaman I and Skandagupta.
Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription is in Sanskrit written in Brahmi script — NOT Kharoshti.
Sudarshana Lake was first built under Chandragupta Maurya; Rudradaman repaired it without forced labour (vishti), via governor Suvishakha; Skandagupta repaired it again c. 455 CE.
Chandragupta II took the title 'Vikramaditya' and 'Sakari' after defeating the Western Kshatrapas (Shakas).
Gandhara sculpture drew on Greco-Roman (Hellenistic) style, flourishing under Shaka-Parthian and Kushana rule.
items.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Junagadh_rock_inscription_of_Rudradaman; standard NCERT/ASI facts on Sudarshana Lake, Chandragupta II Vikramaditya and the Gandhara school
